newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Traders vie for control of Russian oil exports.
newsitem.headline: Traders vie for control of Russian oil exports.

text.p: Both Western and Russian oil traders claimed victory on Friday after the Kremlin changed some rules for exporting Siberian oil, with both sides vowing to dominate the world's third largest crude oil export business.
Western traders said Russia's oil export system was shedding its Byzantine image after a Soviet-type scheme accounting for a chunk of oil exports was scrapped.
But Russians, who have dominated the so-called federal oil export programmes which President Boris Yeltsin eliminated by decree earlier this week, said they were not out of business.
Under the scheme, up to 20 percent of oil was directly exported by powerful Russian trading firms, often with unorthodox political and commercial ties.

"It's not a simple change but it's good for people like ourselves because we'll get more business direct from the producers," said a top Western oil trader. "In fact, our business will probably increase."
But prominent Russian trading outfits had a different view.
"Nobody gives up a market without a fight and we'll still be here," said a source at a top Russian trader.

Federal programmes, in which traders bought oil at low domestic prices, sold it abroad and shared the profit with the government, were axed because domestic energy prices had risen and the scheme no longer offered multi-million dollar profits.
Oil exports are key to the economy, bringing in billions of dollars a year. The cash-strapped state used federal programmes to fund everything from baby-food plants to satellite launches.
The scheme accounted for 15 percent of Russia's total oil exports last year of 2.51 million barrels per day, which included 2.1 million bpd to the West.

But a source at a second prominent Russian trader which did a lot of business with the programmes said the government would not adhere to Yeltsin's decree, because the scheme sometimes financed crucial items in the budget for which there were no alternative sources of revenue.

"It's still too early to say how the decree will be implemented," he said. "My early understanding is federal and intergovernmental programmes will not necessarily be cut but rather be carried out by producers."
Under Yeltsin's decree, federal programmes cease on October 1. The precious pipeline space freed up by their elimination will be available only to producers, not to traders.
"In general, traders will have to rethink their activity in Russia," said Ravil Polyanin, spokesman for Transneft, the state-owned oil pipeline monopoly.
They already have.
"In the future," said the second Russian source, "we may not be able to perform exports under its own name. So we may do so under the name of the oil producer."

The elimination of the programmes does not mean Western traders, who took very little part in the scheme, suffer, since they increasingly work with Russian producers to help them deliver oil to Russian ports, send it abroad and market it.
"They don't mean getting rid of Western oil traders," said the top Western trader. "They mean the special hybrid (of commercial and political interests and of multi-profile firms).

Those companies include Alfa-Eko, Rosnefteimpex and MES, leaders in the federal programme business. The latter organisation, affiliated with the Russian Orthodox Church, exemplified the non-core firms in Russia's oil export game.

"The (Russian oil export) system has become extremely business-oriented and there's no political agenda any more," said the Western trader, saying the scrapping of federal programmes was Moscow's latest step to liberalise the system.
But he wondered if Russia would not find new ways in the future to maximise profits from oil exports.
"We'll probably see some new scheme emerging," he said. "I'm sure we'll see opaque and scandalous programmes in the future."
